With no Threat items present and no active links involving Threat or Triggers, this strategy is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life not worth living anymore' suggests a marked hopeless/depressive or self-destructive appraisal. The rest of the selected items center on fragmented trauma memory and avoidance/social distraction, without other items indicating pervasive defeat, guilt, permanent damage, or a threat-related meaning that would make this severe appraisal cohere strongly.

vignette:
Mateo, a 35-year-old guitarist, described the six months since his accident as living with a constant, low-frequency hum of dread. Before, his life had been defined by rhythm and melody; now, it was defined by noise. The accident itself is a memory he cannot grasp, only endure in pieces. He remembers the glare of headlights in his rearview mirror as he drove home from a late-night gig, the high-pitched squeal of tires on asphalt, and a violent, metallic crunch that seemed to come from inside his own skull. Then, there are only fragments: the smell of gasoline, the sight of the other car's taillights disappearing into the night, the voice of a paramedic asking him questions he couldn't answer. When he deliberately tries to assemble these shards into a coherent narrative, his mind goes blank, as if a curtain has been drawn. He is left with an unsettling sense that the most important parts are missing, lost in the chaotic spin of the impact.

In the weeks that followed, the silence of his apartment, once a comfort, became unbearable. This was where he composed, where he practiced for hours, but now being alone with his thoughts felt dangerous. To fend off the quiet, Mateo began to fill every moment with sound and people. He took on extra gigs, playing in noisy bars he would have previously dismissed. After his own shows, he would insist the band go out, keeping the conversation and laughter going until the early hours of the morning. At home, he would only enter a room if his wife, Sofia, was already there, or if the television was on loud enough to drown out everything else. He found himself unable to talk about what had happened, not with Sofia, not with his bandmates. When they asked, he would offer a tight smile and change the subject, a strategy that felt less like a choice and more like a reflex. The thought of putting the fragmented memories into words was terrifying, as if speaking them aloud would make them solid and inescapable.

This constant motion has come at a cost. His creative work, the very core of his identity, has ground to a halt. He hasn't written a single new piece of music since the accident. The act of composing requires a quiet introspection he can no longer tolerate. This loss has fed a deep and pervasive belief that his life has been irrevocably broken. The person he was-the focused, creative artist-is gone, replaced by this restless, anxious man who can't stand to be alone. This feeling is compounded by a burning sense of injustice. The driver who hit him was never found, a fact that gnaws at him daily. The lack of accountability, of consequence for the person who had upended his world, felt like a profound cosmic unfairness.

This sense of injustice fuels a rage that frightens him more than anything else. On a few occasions, when another driver has cut him off in traffic, he has felt a surge of incandescent fury so powerful it left him shaking. He gripped the steering wheel, his knuckles white, envisioning himself doing something terrible, something violent and uncontrollable. He was certain that if he ever allowed himself to fully connect with the anger simmering just beneath the surface, he would lose control completely and destroy what little he had left. It was Sofia who finally made him seek help. One evening, after he'd spent hours aimlessly channel-surfing to avoid a conversation, she told him, "You're here, but you're not with me. It's like you're afraid of your own home." Her words broke through his wall of avoidance. Mateo has come to therapy not because he wants to remember, but because he is exhausted from running. He is terrified that looking back at the trauma will unleash the rage he has worked so hard to contain, but he holds a fragile hope that he might one day be able to sit in a quiet room with his guitar again and not be afraid of what he might hear in the silence.
